catalog_quote: Sema Lima p. 150: "We can conclude from our data above that Mungaka can be classified as both a register and tone language, as it employs both level and falling/rising tones. [¶] It is also obvious that Mungaka, being a tone language, differs considerably from both English and French, which are stress-timed and syllable-timed, respectively. However, Mungaka-speakers who are bilingual in French and English will agree that Mungaka is perhaps more akin to the former than the latter, not only on the basis of the well-known and interesting coincidence between the French word bon /bon/ for 'good', and the Mungaka word boŋ /boŋ/ for 'good' as well, but also on close similarities in rhythm, both of which are perceived as isosyllabic, unlike English, which is isochronous (i.e., stressed-timed)." | Vielhauer 1915 p. 3: "Die Vokale werden bald lang (ā), bald kurz (a), bald mit Hoch- (á), bald mit Mittel- (a), bald mit Tiefton (à) gesprochen. Es gibt auch noch Zwischentöne, die man aber in der Schrift nicht zu berücksichtigen braucht. Zwei Töne auf einem Vokal hat man bis jetzt erst in der Interjektion ha (ich weiß es nicht) gefunden. Länge- und Tonzeichen werden nur gelegentlich zur Unterscheidung ähnlich klingender Wörter gesetzt."
world_status: statement found in an open source

It is also obvious that Mungaka, being a tone language, differs considerably from both English and French, which are stress-timed and syllable-timed, respectively.. both of which are perceived as isosyllabic, unlike English, which is isochronous (i.e., stressed-timed)."); the compiler ellipsis skips the bo…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Both first-hand descriptions treat Mungaka as a tone language (high/mid/low plus contour tones; tone also grammatical, e.g. future marked by raising the verb tone, Vielhauer p. 102) and give no rule for the location of word stress; Sema Lima only adds that Mungaka rhythm is syllable-based ('isosyllabic'), i.e. not stress-timed. No accessible source states where word stress falls in Mungaka specifically.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any accessible source.
new_statements.exceptions: None. (Vielhauer's 'Betonung/betont' pp. 36-42 concern emphatic pronoun/genitive constructions, not word stress.)
new_statements.domain_note: The only positional stress claim found is genus-level, not Mungaka-specific: Anderson 2001 (in Mutaka & Chumbow eds., Research Mate in African Linguistics, p. 47; saved file), for Eastern Grassfields languages generally (Mungaka explicitly listed under Mbam-Nkam, p. 33; data from Ngiemboon): 'For nouns and verbs with single roots, it appears that the first syllable of the root is stressed. This means that all noun and verb prefixes and any second syllables on the roots are unstressed.' If the catalog admits genus-level inference this would read morphologically determined (root-initial), but it is not a statement about Mungaka data. A Mungaka-specific stress discussion very probably exists in Nti 1986 (Yaoundé thesis; 15 in-volume hits for 'stress', 7 for 'stressed syllable'), which could supersede this compilation.
new_statements.identity_note: All quoted material concerns Mungaka of Bali-Nyonga (mung1266 proper; Vielhauer's 'Balisprache' = Mungaka of Ba'ni Nyonga, explicitly distinguished from the older Mubako' [Chamba] language). Glottolog's two 'phonology' refs (Nusi 2000 Ti; Ngueffo 1979 Bapi) describe the Bati (Ti) and Bapi/Bapakum varieties, not Bali-Nyonga speech. Anderson 2001's stress remark is a genus-level generalization for Eastern Grassfields illustrated from Ngiemboon (ngie1241? no: Ngiemboon = ngie1242), not Mungaka data.

new_statements.quote: p. 22: "Le ti est une langue à tons, c'est-à-dire qu'elle utilise les différences de hauteur de la voix lors de l'exécution des mots pour distinguer des significations. [...] Nous avons relevé deux niveaux de tons ponctuels avec lesquels le parler distingue deux tonèmes : - le tonème haut et - le tonème bas." p. 114: "En ti, il n'existe pas de signes démarcatifs comme c'est le cas avec d'autres langues (l'accent par exemple en [an]glais...) - Cependant, l'analyse des combinaisons révèle un certain nombre de signes démarcatifs fondés sur les incompatibilités. [...] La fonction démarcative n'étant que secondaire, nous ne nous attardons pas dessus."
new_statements.translation: p. 22: "Ti is a tone language, that is, it uses differences in voice pitch during the production of words to distinguish meanings. [...] We have identified two levels of level tones with which the variety distinguishes two tonemes: the high toneme and the low toneme." p. 114: "In Ti there are no demarcative signs such as exist in other languages (accent, for example, in [Eng]lish...) - However, the analysis of combinations reveals a certain number of demarcative signs based on incompatibilities. [...] The demarcative function being only secondary, we do not dwell on it."

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog's existing statement for Mungaka (Sema Lima 1988: tone language, no stress placement): Nusi describes the Ti dialect as tonal and explicitly denies a demarcative accent. The catalog record itself has an empty rule; Nusi adds nothing that would fill it with a stress placement, but confirms the 'tone language, no word-stress statement' reading for the Ti dialect. The word after 'en' on p. 114 is faded on the scan; only '..lais' is legible, so the bracketed 'an' is my reconstruction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ti (a Glottolog dialect of Mungaka) is described as a tone language with high and low level tonemes plus rising and falling contour tones (p. 22-23); the only mention of accent is negative and demarcative: the variety has no boundary-marking accent of the English type, word edges being signalled instead by segmental incompatibilities (glottal stop word-finally, consonant clusters word-initially). No statement of where word stress falls; the work does not treat stress as a word-level category at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the 'demarcative signs' listed are segmental (final glottal stop, initial C+c / N+C clusters), not accentual.
new_statements.identity_note: Nusi 2000 describes Ti, the speech of Bati village (Galim arrondissement, Bamboutos, West Region), which Glottolog lists as dialect tiii1240 of mung1266; the author calls Mungaka 'parler le plus proche du ti' and reports mutual intelligibility, and cites Vielhauer's account that Mungaka arose from contact between Ti and the Chamba language Mubakoh. Ngueffo 1979 describes Bapi, a village 15 km north-west of Bafoussam (neighbours Bamougoum, Bandeng, Baleng, Bafou'nda), grouped by Hombert 1977 with Bamoun and Bandeng in the Noun group; it is not a Glottolog dialect of Mungaka and the thesis never mentions Mungaka or Bali, so its attachment to mung1266 in the listing is at best a sister-variety link.

The high tone is unmarked e.g a “it”, the ,.lay, tone is marked e.g iIa-L‘‘which” and … the mid tone is also marked . m:cperfect … aspect marker”. tone_statements.summary: Five phonemic tones: three level (high, low, mid) and two contour (falling, rising); high tone left unmarked; imperative, adhortative and optative moods marked by a high tone. Nothing on word stress.
